title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Kalamazoo adds a moratorium while residents statewide weigh power, water and farmland impacts.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's a sunny Saturday morning here on September 5, 2026, and we're diving straight into the latest moves slowing the data center boom across the state.
That's right — Kalamazoo just added a moratorium to its zoning code, and it feels like the start of a bigger conversation about how fast these projects are moving.
Exactly. Officials there are writing a temporary ban on new data centers into the local rules as AI-driven proposals keep multiplying.
Why now? What sparked this decision in Kalamazoo specifically?

Residents could see fewer projects competing for power and land while the township studies the real impacts. It comes right amid those statewide worries about grid strain and water use from large facilities.
So this isn't happening in a vacuum. We've seen similar pauses popping up elsewhere recently.
Right. Garfield Township decided yesterday to spend a full year crafting its own data center rules, and Lakeshore Township blocked projects using existing zoning just yesterday too.
What does a moratorium actually buy the community in practical terms?
Time to look at how these facilities pull hundreds of megawatts, millions of gallons of water daily, and what that does to local electric rates and aquifers.
And the farmland angle — these projects often target rural spots. How does that play into the Kalamazoo decision?
It keeps new builds from racing ahead before folks can weigh the trade-offs on taxes, traffic, noise, and lost agricultural land.
Who are the main players here? Local officials, residents, or the developers pushing these AI campuses?
All three. Township leaders are responding to resident pushback while developers look for spots with available power and water.
What happens next in Kalamazoo? Is this a short pause or could it stretch longer?
The temporary ban gives them breathing room to study impacts, and other townships are already watching to see if similar language works for them.
We've got that Mid-Michigan town hall from yesterday too — residents getting concrete numbers on megawatts and daily water use.
Yes, a university-hosted session laying out exactly how proposed centers could hit local electricity rates and aquifer levels for anyone within 30 miles.
That kind of transparency seems key. Does the Kalamazoo move signal more of that coming?
It looks like it. The delay lets locals question developers before anything advances, which echoes what we're hearing in Ypsilanti and Washtenaw County.
Speaking of which, activists are protesting today over water use at two proposed campuses that could draw millions of gallons daily.
Right — the Saturday event at the Van Buren Township line targets those projects, and homeowners in Washtenaw and Wayne counties have a direct stake in the outcome.
How does this tie into broader grid concerns? Ionia was talking yesterday about letting centers tap city power.
Council members there discussed inviting facilities that could pull hundreds of megawatts, with residents 30 miles away potentially seeing higher utility bills if new plants or lines are needed.
No vote yet, but the signal is they're open. Meanwhile, a farm in another area is seeking annexation to build on rural land.
That one would shift tax revenue and local control away from the township, changing land use for folks even 30 miles out.
And then there's the University of Michigan computing center drawing fire over possible nuclear weapons ties.
Ann Arbor residents and activists want clearer answers on how the project could support military programs, affecting state research funding and local oversight.
Transparency keeps coming up. Lenox Township residents on Thursday were demanding full disclosure after learning details only through back channels.
They're worried about noise, power strain, and lost farmland in Macomb County, and those transparency failures are fueling distrust.
A recall bid tied to rezoning failed again on Thursday too. How does that fit the bigger picture?
The fight centers on land-use changes that could open the door to large-scale farms, and voters nearby are watching how it shapes future development battles.
So across the state, we're seeing this mix of pauses, protests, and push for answers. What should listeners take away from Kalamazoo's move today?
It shows communities aren't just reacting — they're getting ahead of the rush by studying the real costs on power, water, and land before more projects lock in.
And with AI demand only growing, these local decisions could set the template for the rest of Michigan.
We'll keep tracking how the studies play out and whether other townships follow suit.
Shifting to quick hits now — Garfield Township is taking a full year to draft its own zoning and permitting standards.
That gives Grand Traverse County residents time to weigh limits on power demand, noise, and water use before any project moves forward.
Lakeshore Township used existing rules yesterday to block data centers near homes and wells, keeping those impacts off the table for now.
Nearby west Michigan towns are watching closely to see if the same ordinances work for them.
Mid-Michigan got its first detailed look at power and water demands at that university town hall yesterday.
Residents within 30 miles heard concrete numbers and got a chance to question developers directly.
Ypsilanti-area activists are gathering today to protest water use at two proposed campuses.
The event targets projects that could draw millions of gallons daily, with Washtenaw and Wayne county homeowners within driving distance.
A rural property owner is pushing for city annexation to build a data center on farmland.
That would shift tax revenue and local control, affecting land use for residents 30 miles away if it succeeds.
University of Michigan's new computing facility is raising questions about possible nuclear weapons work ties.
Ann Arbor activists want clearer answers on military program support and how it affects local oversight.
Lenox Township residents demanded full disclosure on Thursday after learning of plans through back channels.
They're concerned about noise, power strain, and farmland loss in Macomb County.
A second recall attempt failed for an official tied to data center rezoning.
The dispute centers on land-use changes, and nearby voters are watching the outcome.
Ionia discussed inviting data centers that could tap city power and land yesterday.
No vote yet, but the talk signals openness — with potential bill impacts for residents 30 miles out.
On deck for listeners — any meetings worth marking on the calendar?
No major public sessions listed for today or tomorrow in the tracker, but township agendas often update quickly.
Folks should check their local boards for any last-minute notices on zoning or studies.
We'll flag anything new in tomorrow's episode.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow with the latest.
Thanks for listening — stay informed out there.

episode_title: Kalamazoo Pauses Data Center Rush as Grid and Water Concerns Grow
